docs.title: Rig Tools
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

RigTools is a Blender 4.0+ add-on for building character rigs one piece at a time. Instead of generating a whole rig from a metarig, you select a chain of bones and build an assembly on it: an arm, a leg, a torso, a skirt, a tail. Assemblies can be reconfigured or deleted later, so the rig never gets locked into an uneditable state.

Version 1 is centered around humanoid characters.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Install: Edit > Preferences > Add-ons > Install > select rigtools.zip

Find it: View3D > Sidebar (n-panel) > Rig Tools, with an armature selected.

Then follow the Workflow from an empty scene to a finished rig.

docs.title: Armature Settings
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Each armature stores a few bone names that RigTools needs to know about: the root, the property bone, and the torso bones. These are set in the Armature Settings panel.

Where: n-Panel > RigTools > Armature Settings

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The first time RigTools is used on an armature, the armature settings are filled in from the addon preferences. After that, each armature keeps its own settings, so different rigs can use different names.

Reinitialize from Preferences resets the armature's settings back to the current addon preferences.

Warning

The property bone must exist before any assemblies are created. The assembly will fail with an error if it can't be found. The RigTools Human Skeleton includes a root and property bone. If you're building your own skeleton, create these bones before creating assemblies.

Image placeholder

image/armature_settings.png — The Armature Settings panel in the RigTools n-panel with the default bone names filled in, plus the Reinitialize from Preferences button.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Description Root root The root bone of the rig. Used for IK controls, rotation isolation, and the torso. Torso torso Name of the torso control. Created by the torso assembly. Used as an IK parent. Hips hips Name of the hips control. Created by the torso assembly. Used as an IK parent. Chest chest Name of the chest control. Created by the torso assembly. Used as an IK parent. Head head Name of the head control. Created by the torso assembly. Used as an IK parent. Property properties The property bone.

The torso, hips, chest, and head bones don't need to exist ahead of time. The torso assembly creates them using these names, and the IK parent switching uses the same names to find them. This is why the torso should be set up before the arms, legs, and spline assemblies.

docs.title: Property bone
docs.text:
The property bone holds all of the custom properties that animators use to control the rig: FK/IK switches, rotation isolation, IK parents, IK stretch, and skirt collision and ride. These are displayed in the Rig Properties panel.

The property bone is usually placed above the character's head, and doesn't deform. Apply Root Widgets gives it a gear widget and locks its transforms.

Warning

Don't rename the property bone after assemblies have been created. The rig's drivers and the Rig Properties panel look for properties on this bone.

docs.title: Upgrade Rig
docs.text:
Occasionally, an update to RigTools changes the data it stores on the armature. When an older rig is opened with a newer version of RigTools, an Upgrade Rig button appears at the top of the Armature Settings panel and the Assembly Panel. Click it to update the rig's data.

Tip

Save a backup of the file before upgrading the rig.

docs.title: Addon Preferences
docs.text:
Where: Edit > Preferences > Add-ons > Rig Tools

The addon preferences set the defaults for new rigs. Changing the preferences doesn't change existing armatures; use Reinitialize from Preferences for that.

Export Settings... and Import Settings... save and load the preferences as a JSON file. This is useful for sharing settings between machines or Blender versions.

docs.title: Quick Bone Selection
docs.text:
• Selection Buttons: comma-separated list of the quick selection buttons. Default: FK, IK-, Tweak, DEF, ORG, MCH.
  • Columns: the number of columns for the selection buttons. Default: 3.

docs.title: Name Stripping
docs.text:
• Tags to Strip: comma-separated list of prefixes and suffixes removed from bone names when RigTools names new bones. Default: ORG, DEF, MCH, CTRL. For example, ORG-forearm.L becomes FK-forearm.L instead of FK-ORG-forearm.L.
  • Separators: the characters that separate tags from the rest of the name. Default: -._

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
• DEF Bone: the naming template for deform bones. Default: DEF-{name}.
  • Target/ORG Bone: the naming template for ORG bones. Default: ORG-{name}.
  • FK Bone: the naming template for FK controls. Default: FK-{name}.

{name} is replaced with the base name of the bone. .L / .R suffixes are always kept at the end of the name. These are used by Generate ORG Bones and the assemblies.

docs.title: Rig Structure Defaults
docs.text:
• Root Bone, Torso Bone, Hips Bone, Chest Bone, Head Bone, Property Bone: the defaults for the armature settings above.
  • Non-Limb MCH Collection: the bone collection for mechanism bones that don't belong to a limb. Default: MCH-TMP.
  • MCH Parent Collection: the parent collection for all MCH bone collections. Default: MCH.
  • Widget Collection: the scene collection where widgets are created. Default: WGT.

docs.title: Control Colors
docs.text:
The bone color sets used for each type of control.

  • FK Color: default Theme 4.
  • IK Color: default Theme 1.
  • Master Control Color: used for the root, torso controls, master controllers, and other special controls. Default Theme 2.
  • Tweak Color: default Theme 9.

docs.title: Assemblies
docs.text:
One of the core operations with RigTools is the creation of "Assemblies". For many purposes, an assembly is often analogous with a limb, like an arm or a leg. You can create full arm and leg assemblies really quickly and easily. Assemblies aren't restricted to just limbs, though, and you can potentially stack multiple assemblies on a single limb.

Start here

Assemblies are the main unit of rig building in Rig Tools. Read this page before the individual tool pages.

docs.title: Selection
docs.text:
Requires

Armature selected · Edit or Pose mode · linear bone chain(s)

All assemblies start with a selection. That selection needs to be one or more linear chains of bones. When starting, it may be easier to think of it as a single chain of bones, but all assemblies allow you to select multiple chains and it will create one assembly per chain. For some assemblies, it might not make a lot of sense to do that, but for others it will.

Important

A chain is a sequence of bones linked by parenting: each bone (except the first) is a child of the previous one. Order runs from the root of the sequence toward the tip. A linear chain is a chain with no branching within the selection. At every step of the chain there is at most one child.

Example of several simple linear chains for a skirt.

Bones in a chain do not need to be connected. RigTools only cares about parenting, which establishes bone order. If you have a chain that branches, such as hair with off-shoots, you can use the selection to tell RigTools which bones make up a chain.

Invalid chain - The third bone has three children. Valid chain - several of these bones have more than one child, but they aren't part of the selection

In this hair example, the main chain for the hair can be used to create an assembly. The bones for the bow and the flyaways can be used to make another assembly, or be rigged manually.

The tools Select Hierarchy and Select Connected can be used to help select chains. They are particularly useful for selecting multiple chains. The "Select Connected" tool can be useful for selecting just the connected parts of a branching chain.

docs.title: Reversible
docs.text:
All assemblies are reversible -- to a point.

When you create a new assembly, RigTools will save all the data about that assembly, including how to reverse it. Assemblies can be deleted or reconfigured after they are created.

Important Caveat

You cannot delete or reconfigure an assembly if another assembly depends on it. RigTools checks automatically for dependencies and prevents this from happening. Deleting or reconfiguring will also delete any manual changes made and any manual dependencies you create will be orphaned.

Assembly dependencies usually require that another assembly reference the control bones of another assembly, so it shouldn't happen in most normal circumstances.

Note that reconfiguring is just deleting and recreating. It's not doing anything special to preserve existing bones.

With these important caveats, this is still a really powerful tool. It's probably best to think of it in the context of added flexibility within a short window of time. You can try out an assembly and not have to worry about setting all the way back through a long undo buffer. There also may be some times where it's still safe to reconfigure an assembly much later. And sometimes, you might even know you're going to lose something and it's still the best solution. By keeping track of all the assemblies and allowing you to delete them, RigTools maintains that flexibility.

Deleting or reconfiguring an assembly will not delete any bone collections that were created. This is done intentionally to preserve Rig UI data and other bone collection states. Blender offers the "Remove Unused" tool in the Bone Collections tab, if you need to remove any orphaned collections. All other parts of the assemblies are deleted, including: bones (excluding twist bones), custom properties, widgets, splines, etc.

docs.title: Creating Assemblies
docs.text:
After you've selected the correct bone chain, you can create a new assembly by clicking on one of the templates in RigTools n-panel. Currently, there are two sections of the n-panel that include templates: "Inverse Kinematics" and "Forward Kinematics". Both of these panels include templates for creating assemblies. The tools used behind the scenes are slightly different, and the Inverse Kinematics are generally more complex and include FK/IK switching. Forward kinematics are generally simpler chains that don't include IK constraints.

The "Forward Kinematics" section also includes buttons for a few special assemblies: Torso (spine, neck, and head), Shoulder, and Palm.

This list will almost certainly be expanded in the future

Image placeholder

image/templates.png may need to be updated — it should show the current Inverse Kinematics and Forward Kinematics sections, including the Torso, Finger (Curl), Finger (FK), Shoulder, and Palm buttons.

The templates are one-click tools that generate the assembly immediately using a sensible set of defaults, while still offering a redo panel with a trimmed-down set of settings that are focused on the specific assembly type. Pick the template that most closely resembles what you're working on. The Palm template is the exception: it opens a dialog first, so you can confirm the order of the palm bones.

Redo panel after creating an Arm IK Assembly (specific settings subject to change)

docs.title: Assembly Panel
docs.text:
After you create an assembly, it will show up in the Assembly Panel. The Assembly Panel will show all assemblies associated with the selected bones. If you select all the bones in the rig, it will show you all assemblies.

Note

The UI of the Assembly Panel is likely to change in the near future

From this panel, you can reconfigure an assembly or delete it.

Warning

Reconfiguring an assembly will delete it and then create it. This comes with the same caveats as deleting.

docs.title: Forward Kinematics Assemblies
docs.text:
FK assemblies build control chains without a full IK stack: FK bones, optional tweaks, optional rotation isolation / master controllers (rotation follow), and a dedicated Torso template for spine–neck–head. There are also options for skirt collision and ride on the Skirt FK template.

Requires

Read Assemblies first for selection, templates, and delete/reconfigure rules. For twist details on Torso, see Twist Bones.

Requires

Armature selected · Edit or Pose mode · linear ORG chain(s)

docs.title: How to run
docs.text:
1. Select one or more linear chains (typically ORG bones — see ORG & DEF).
  2. Open the Forward Kinematics section of the Rig Tools n-panel.
  3. Click an FK template button.

docs.title: When to use FK vs IK
docs.text:
Use FK assemblies Use IK assemblies Fingers, tails, simple cloth, hair strands Arms, legs, anything that needs poles / IK goals You only want FK + tweaks You need FK/IK switching and snapping Torso / spine–neck–head Spline IK skirts/hair/tails when you specifically want splines

Use FK assemblies when you have simple mechanisms that don't require IK. Generally, arm and legs should use IK assemblies. The spline IK assemblies are available, but are generally special-case uses. Consider using FK first for hair, cloth, tails, etc., and switch to IK if you can't get the results you want.

docs.title: Torso
docs.text:
Note

The torso assembly includes the head and neck, not just the spine. All head and neck bones should be included in the selection.

Torso is a special assembly type with a torso FK tool that is specifically built for constructing a torso.

The default torso configuration includes 6 bones: ORG-hips, ORG-spine.01, ORG-spine.02, ORG-chest, ORG-neck, and ORG-head (or similar). The hips and spine.01 are the lower torso bones, and will be controlled by a hips controller. The spine.02 and chest bones are the upper torso bones, and will be controlled by a chest controller. These default settings are configurable. For more information, see torso FK.

  • Builds master controls: torso, hips, chest, plus FK along the spine/neck and a head control (names from armature settings).
  • Optional tweaks along the chain (including over twist subdivisions).
  • Optional neck and chest twist bones.
  • Optional neck / head rotation isolation (separate properties; on by default).
  • Neck falloff so neck twists / FKs can ease toward the head (default: root).

Note

Torso creates the hips/chest/torso/head controls that IK parent tools will reference later. Set up torso before other IK assemblies.

The torso includes the option for twist bones on the chest and neck. The chest twist bones won't actually twist (see torso FK for more information), they just provide an additional tweak controller on the chest. The neck twist bones do twist, following the head. The default fall-off setting is "root" (slightly softer than "sharp"). It is recommended to use the default setting of 1 neck bone with 2 twist bones for most humanoid characters. For characters with longer necks, see torso FK.

Image placeholder

image/fk_torso.png — A finished Torso assembly in Pose mode, showing the torso, hips, chest, neck, and head controls.

docs.title: Simple FK
docs.text:
The Simple FK assembly is a general-purpose FK chain with tweaks. Use it for hair strands, cloth strips, or any chain that does not need a specialized template.

  • Creates an FK/Tweak chain with circle widgets by default.
  • Master Controllers are enabled as FK follow from the second bone (skip first).
  • Rotation Isolation is available but off by default.

docs.title: FK Only
docs.text:
Same idea as Simple FK, but without tweak bones — especially useful for short (1-2 bone) chains.

  • Creates FK controls only (no tweaks).
  • Master Controllers are enabled as FK follow from the second bone (skip first).
  • Rotation Isolation is available but off by default.

docs.title: Skirt FK
docs.text:
Requires

Skirt collision / ride reference leg bones. Set up both leg assemblies first for easier setup.

The Skirt FK assembly is intended for skirts and dresses. There is also a Skirt - Spline IK template when you specifically want spline IK; Skirt FK is usually preferable.

  • Creates an FK/Tweak chain with rectangle widgets.
  • Rotation Isolation is enabled by default.
  • Skirt Collision is enabled by default.
  • Skirt Ride is intended for short skirts (the tendency for short skirts to ride up when the leg is lifted). It is disabled by default.
  • Master Controllers are enabled as master controllers from the second bone (skip first).

Image placeholder

image/fk_skirt.png — A finished Skirt FK assembly in Pose mode, showing the rectangle FK widgets and the master controls, with one leg raised so the skirt collision is visible.

docs.title: Tail
docs.text:
The Tail assembly is an FK setup for tails. There is also a Tail - Spline IK template; choice is largely preference and may depend on tail length.

  • Creates an FK/Tweak chain with circle widgets; limb base name defaults to tail.
  • Rotation Isolation is enabled by default.
  • Master Controllers are enabled every 3 bones (skipping the first), as master controllers.

Image placeholder

image/fk_tail.png — A finished Tail assembly in Pose mode, showing the FK controls, tweaks, and a master control every 3 bones, with one master rotated so the tail curls.

docs.title: Finger (FK)
docs.text:
The Finger (FK) assembly is a compact FK chain for fingers. It skips the first tweak so a metacarpal (or similar root) can sit without an extra tweak at the base.

  • Creates an FK/Tweak chain with circle widgets; skips the first tweak by default.
  • Master Controllers are enabled as FK follow from the second bone (skip first).

Apply fingers separately after an Arm assembly; the arm template does not build palms or fingers.

docs.title: Finger (Curl)
docs.text:
The Finger (Curl) assembly is an alternative to Finger (FK), similar to Rigify's finger controls. Each finger gets a single, larger curl control: rotate it to rotate the whole finger, and scale it down to curl the finger.

  • Creates an FK/Tweak chain with circle widgets; skips the first tweak by default.
  • Adds a finger curl control. The curl axis is detected automatically, and can be changed in the redo panel.
  • Master Controllers are not used.

Image placeholder

image/fk_fingers_compare.png — Side-by-side of one hand with Finger (FK) assemblies and one with Finger (Curl) assemblies, showing the difference in controls (FK circles vs. a single curl control per finger).

docs.title: Shoulder
docs.text:
Requires

Select only the shoulder bone. The arm should be a separate Arm assembly.

The Shoulder assembly creates a single FK control for a humanoid shoulder (clavicle).

  • Creates a shoulder FK control with a shoulder widget, drawn above the shoulder so it's easy to grab.
  • The shoulder is grouped with the arm on the same side, and its control is visible in both the arm's FK and IK bone collections.

docs.title: Palm
docs.text:
Requires

Select the palm bones (one per finger), not a chain. Both hands can be selected at once.

The Palm assembly creates FK controls for the palm bones. Unlike the other assemblies, the palm bones aren't a chain, so the Palm assembly opens a dialog to confirm the order of the bones, from index to pinky.

  • Creates a palm FK control for each palm bone, with pill widgets.
  • The first (index) and last (pinky) palms also control the palms between them, with a falloff. This makes cupping and spreading the hand easy with only two controls.

docs.title: Inverse Kinematics Assemblies
docs.text:
IK assemblies build a limb with FK/IK switching and additional options. Additional options include tweak controls (on by default), FK rotation isolation, FK master controllers, IK parent switching, FK<>IK snapping, and additional mechanisms for skirt collision and ride. There are also options for spline IK, on top of the standard arm/leg IK setups. Spline IK setups do not include FK<>IK snapping, as it is often impossible for the spline IK to match an FK chain.

Requires

Read Assemblies first for selection, templates, and delete/reconfigure rules. For twist details, see Twist Bones.

Requires

Armature selected · Edit or Pose mode · linear ORG chain(s)

docs.title: How to run
docs.text:
1. Select one or more linear chains (typically ORG bones — see ORG & DEF).
  2. Open the Inverse Kinematics section of the Rig Tools n-panel.
  3. Click an IK template button.

docs.title: Arm
docs.text:
Requires

Requires a torso to be set up first. It will reference torso bones for IK parenting.

The Arm assembly is a standard setup for a humanoid arm. In most cases, the chain should be exactly 3 bones (arm, forearm, hand). The arm assembly does not include additional mechanisms for the palms or fingers. Those should be applied separately (see FK Assemblies).

  • Creates a standard IK setup with 2 IK bones, a pole, and the hand as the control.
  • Includes FK/IK switching and FK/Tweak controls.
  • FK <> IK Snapping is set up automatically.
  • Rotation Isolation is available and enabled by default.

Arms can include twist bones, as is often desirable for a high-quality rig. Twist bones can be set up ahead of time, or the tool will add them automatically if the setting is enabled. It is recommended to set them up ahead of time so they can be weight painted with the rest of the rig. By default it uses 4 twist bones each for the arm and forearm, with "root" falloff on the upper arm (slightly softer than "sharp") and "linear" falloff on the forearm. These are decent defaults for most models and can be tweaked as needed.

The arm template automatically sets up IK parent switching with root, torso, hips, chest, and head as parent targets. The torso must be set up first so those bones exist. IK parents can be adjusted without reconfiguring the assembly.

Image placeholder

image/ik_arm.png — A finished Arm assembly side by side in FK and in IK, showing the FK controls, the IK hand control, the pole target, and the tweaks.

docs.title: Leg
docs.text:
Requires

Requires a torso to be set up first. It will be referenced for IK parenting.

The Leg assembly is a standard setup for a humanoid leg. The chain should be exactly 4 bones long (thigh, shin, foot, toe). Include the toe even when you are not using foot roll.

  • Creates a standard IK setup with 2 IK bones, a pole, and the foot as the control.
  • Includes FK/IK switching and FK/Tweak controls, plus an additional FK control for the toe.
  • Foot roll is enabled by default (requires a heel pivot).
  • FK <> IK Snapping is set up automatically.
  • Rotation Isolation is available and enabled by default.

Legs can include twist bones, as is often desirable for a high-quality rig. Twist bones can be set up ahead of time, or the tool will add them automatically if the setting is enabled. It is recommended to set them up ahead of time so they can be weight painted with the rest of the rig. By default it uses 4 twist bones each for the thigh and shin, with "sharp" falloff on the thigh and no falloff on the shin. The shin does not typically twist on most rigs, but the twist bones are included by default for consistency and for the additional tweak bones. These are decent defaults for most models and can be tweaked as needed.

The leg template automatically sets up IK parent switching with root, torso, and foot as parent targets for the legs. A torso must be set up first. The "foot" option parents the pole to the foot, and the foot is parented to the root. IK parents can be adjusted without reconfiguring the assembly.

Image placeholder

image/ik_leg.png — A finished Leg assembly in IK, showing the flattened IK foot control, the foot roll control, the knee pole, and the toe control.

docs.title: Skirt - Spline
docs.text:
Requires

Requires a torso and hips bones to be set up first. These bones will be referenced for IK parenting.

Image placeholder

image/ik_splines.png — The three spline templates (Skirt - Spline, Hair - Spline, Tail - Spline) in IK mode, showing their sphere controls and twist controllers along each chain.

The skirt assembly is a spline IK setup intended for skirts and dresses. There is also a Skirt FK setup that may be more desirable in most cases. Skirt - Spline adds extra complexity and should only be used when spline IK is desirable.

  • Creates a spline IK setup with 3 controllers and twist controls at the start and end.
  • Includes FK/IK switching and FK/Tweak controls.
  • Rotation Isolation is available and enabled by default.
  • Skirt Collision is enabled by default.
  • Skirt Ride is intended for short skirts (the tendency for short skirts to ride up when the leg is lifted). It is disabled by default.
  • Master Controllers can be set up. The default configuration is FK follow from the second bone in the chain (skip first).

Spline IK limitations

Spline IK assemblies do not support limb twist bones (they use spline twist controllers instead) or FK <> IK snapping (a spline IK pose often cannot match an FK chain).

The skirt template automatically sets up IK parent switching with root, torso, and hips as parent targets. The torso and hips bones must be set up first. IK parents can be adjusted without reconfiguring the assembly.

docs.title: Hair - Spline
docs.text:
Requires

Requires a torso and head bones to be set up first. These bones will be referenced for IK parenting.

The hair assembly is a spline IK setup intended for long hair, especially ponytails and pigtails. A Simple FK setup is usually more desirable for most hair. Hair - Spline adds extra complexity and should only be used when spline IK is desirable.

  • Creates a spline IK setup with 3 controllers and twist controls at every control point.
  • Includes FK/IK switching and FK/Tweak controls.
  • Rotation Isolation is available and enabled by default.
  • Master Controllers can be set up. The default configuration is FK follow from the second bone in the chain (skip first).

Spline IK limitations

Spline IK assemblies do not support limb twist bones (they use spline twist controllers instead) or FK <> IK snapping (a spline IK pose often cannot match an FK chain).

The hair template automatically sets up IK parent switching with root, torso, and head as parent targets. The torso and head bones must be set up first. IK parents can be adjusted without reconfiguring the assembly.

docs.title: Tail - Spline
docs.text:
Requires

Requires a torso and hips bones to be set up first. These bones will be referenced for IK parenting.

The tail assembly is a spline IK setup intended for long tails. There is also a Tail FK that may be more desirable for some tails. This is largely preference and may depend on tail length.

  • Creates a spline IK setup with 4 controllers and twist controls at the beginning and end.
  • Includes FK/IK switching and FK/Tweak controls.
  • Rotation Isolation is available and enabled by default.
  • Master Controllers can be set up. The default configuration is master controllers every 3 bones (skipping the first).

Spline IK limitations

Spline IK assemblies do not support limb twist bones (they use spline twist controllers instead) or FK <> IK snapping (a spline IK pose often cannot match an FK chain).

The tail template automatically sets up IK parent switching with root, torso, and hips as parent targets. The torso and hips bones must be set up first. IK parents can be adjusted without reconfiguring the assembly.

docs.title: ORG & DEF
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

RigTools splits the skeleton into two layers: DEF bones that deform the mesh, and ORG bones that the assemblies are built on. The DEF bones follow the ORG bones.

Tip

Assemblies are created on ORG chains. When selecting a chain for an assembly, select the ORG bones.

docs.title: Why two layers?
docs.text:
The DEF bones are the ones that are weight painted. Keeping them separate from the rig mechanics means:

  • Assemblies can be created, deleted, and reconfigured without touching the weight painting.
  • The DEF bones stay in a simple hierarchy that's easy to export to game engines and other tools.
  • New DEF bones (an accessory, a skirt, a ponytail) can be added later, and ORG bones generated for just those.
Layer Role DEF Deform bones. The mesh is weight painted to these. ORG The bones assemblies are built on. Don't deform. The DEF bones follow these. Controls / MCH Created by the assemblies: FK, IK, tweaks, and the mechanism (MCH) bones that make them work.

Image placeholder

image/org_def_layers.png — An arm shown three ways: the DEF bones only, the ORG bones only, and the finished arm with FK/IK controls and tweaks visible.

docs.title: Typical order
docs.text:
1. Build the DEF skeleton, or start from the RigTools Human Skeleton.
  2. Optionally, add twist bones and assign heel pivots.
  3. Weight paint the DEF bones.
  4. Run Generate ORG Bones.
  5. Select ORG chains and create the torso, then the IK and FK assemblies.
  6. Animate with the Rig UI.

See Workflow for the full process.

docs.title: Generate ORG Bones
docs.text:
Generate ORG Bones creates an ORG bone for each DEF bone, with the same hierarchy, and makes the DEF bone follow it with a Copy Transforms constraint. It's safe to run more than once; only the missing ORG bones are created.

Twist bone and heel pivot assignments made on the DEF bones are copied to the ORG bones.

docs.title: Heel pivots
docs.text:
Foot roll on the Leg assembly needs a heel pivot bone assigned to the foot.

  • Assign it in Bone Properties > Rig Tools > Heel Pivot, with the foot bone active (not the toe).
  • Assign it on the DEF foot before running Generate ORG Bones, or on the ORG foot before creating the leg.

See Foot Roll for where to place the heel pivot.

Image placeholder

image/bone_properties_rigtools.png — The Rig Tools section of Bone Properties with a foot bone active, showing the Twist Parent field and the Heel Pivot field.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text: RigTools uses the bone names to tell DEF and ORG bones apart, and to name the bones it creates. The defaults are DEF-{name} and ORG-{name}, with .L / .R suffixes kept at the end. For example, DEF-forearm.L and ORG-forearm.L. The naming templates can be changed in the addon preferences.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Keep DEF and ORG naming consistent so Generate ORG Bones and the assemblies can find the right bones.
  • Create twist bones on the DEF bones and weight paint them before generating ORG bones. The assemblies will use the existing twist bones, as long as the twist bone count matches.
  • Bone parenting is what makes a chain. If your DEF chain isn't parented correctly, the ORG chain won't be either. See Parent Along Chain.

docs.title: Selection
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Tools for selecting bones and chains. Every assembly starts with a selection, so these come up a lot.

Where: n-Panel > RigTools > Selection (Edit or Pose mode)

Image placeholder

image/selection_panel.png — The Selection panel showing the quick select buttons, the search field, and the Select Connected / Select Mirror buttons.

docs.title: Quick select buttons
docs.text:
A grid of buttons that select every visible bone whose name contains the button's text. For example, FK selects all visible bones with "FK" in the name. Matching is not case sensitive, and the buttons add to the current selection.

The buttons can be changed in the addon preferences. The default buttons are FK, IK-, Tweak, DEF, ORG, MCH.

Below the buttons is a search field. Type part of a bone name and click the select button next to it to select all visible bones that contain that text.

Tip

Hide the bone collections you don't want, then use a quick select button. For example, show only the ORG collections and click ORG to select all of the ORG bones.

docs.title: Select Connected
docs.text:
Extends the selection down the chain from each selected bone, following children that are connected to their parent. It stops at bones that aren't connected, and at hidden bones.

This is useful for selecting several chains at once: select the first bone of each chain, then click Select Connected. It's also useful for branching chains, like hair with flyaways, where only the connected part of the chain should be selected.

docs.title: Select Mirror
docs.text: Adds the opposite side of each selected bone to the selection. For example, selecting the left leg chain and clicking Select Mirror also selects the right leg chain, so both legs can be created as assemblies at the same time.

docs.title: Select Hierarchy
docs.text:
Blender's built-in hierarchy selection is also useful for chains, particularly when the bones aren't connected:

  • Pose mode: Select > Child / Extend Child (] / Shift+])
  • Edit mode: Select > Child / Extend Child (] / Shift+])

Extend Child adds the next bone down the chain to the selection. Repeat it to walk down the chain one bone at a time.

docs.title: Twist Bones
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Twist bones spread a twist along a limb, so the forearm twists smoothly from the wrist to the elbow instead of all at once at the wrist. They're deform bones, not animator controls.

The Arm, Leg, and Torso assemblies use twist bones. They can create the twist bones for you, or use twist bones you've already created. Each twist bone also gets a tweak control, which gives the animator extra controls along the limb.

Start here

Twist bones are set up by the assemblies. Read Assemblies first if you haven't.

Not spline twist

Spline IK has its own twist controllers on the spline. That's a separate feature; see Spline IK.

Image placeholder

image/twist_bones.png — A forearm with 4 twist bones, shown with the hand rotated 90 degrees so the twist is visibly spread along the forearm. Ideally side-by-side with the same pose and no twist bones (candy-wrapper deformation at the wrist).

docs.title: Twist parent
docs.text:
RigTools doesn't rely on bone names to know which bones are twist bones. Instead, each twist bone is assigned a twist parent: the bone it belongs to. For example, the forearm twist bones have the forearm as their twist parent.

The twist bones for one bone must form a single chain, parented from the start of the bone to the end.

The twist parent of the active bone can be viewed and changed in Bone Properties > Rig Tools > Twist Parent. The panel also lists the twist bones that belong to the active bone.

To assign many twist bones at once, select the twist bones, then select the twist parent last so it's the active bone, and use Set Twist Parent (Ctrl+Shift+P) from the Edit mode Armature > Parent menu. Clear Twist Parent (Ctrl+Alt+P) removes the assignment. Both work with X-Axis Mirror, so the other side is assigned at the same time.

Note

Generate ORG Bones copies twist parents from the DEF bones to the ORG bones. Twist bones created on the DEF bones will carry over.

docs.title: Creating twist bones
docs.text:
Twist bones can be created three ways:

  1. Create Twist Bones: the Create Twist Bones tool splits each selected DEF bone into twist bones. This is the recommended approach, since the twist bones can be weight painted along with the rest of the rig.
  2. By the assembly: if an assembly needs twist bones and none exist, it creates them, both DEF and ORG. The new DEF twist bones will need to be weight painted.
  3. Manually: create the bones yourself, parent them into a chain, and assign their twist parent. This is useful for custom layouts.

docs.title: Deleting assemblies
docs.text:
When an assembly is deleted or reconfigured, its twist bones are kept, so the weight painting isn't lost. The next assembly will use the same twist bones.

Twist bone count

If twist bones already exist for a bone, the assembly's twist bone count must match. Otherwise, the assembly fails with an error. The redo panel shows the status of the twist bones before the assembly is created.

docs.title: Arm and Leg
docs.text:
The Arm and Leg assemblies use twist bones by default, on the upper arm and forearm, or the thigh and shin. The twist is picked up from the controls, and fades along each segment.

Assembly Segment Twist from Falloff Twist bones Arm Upper arm Upper arm Root 4 Arm Forearm Hand Linear 4 Leg Thigh Thigh Sharp 4 Leg Shin (none) — 4

The shin twist bones don't twist by default. They're included for consistency, and for the additional tweak controls.

See Twist Bones (tool) for the parameters, and what each falloff does.

docs.title: Torso
docs.text: The torso has optional twist bones on the chest and the neck (2 each by default). The neck twist bones follow the head, with the falloff set by Neck Falloff. The chest twist bones don't twist; they add an extra tweak control to the chest. See Torso FK.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
Image placeholder

image/workflow_finished_rig.png — A finished character rig in Pose mode (torso, arms, legs, fingers, and a skirt or hair assembly), with the Rig UI panel open. Shows where the workflow ends up.

  1. Create the initial rig skeleton:

    Add > Armature > RigTools Human Skeleton Use this base skeleton, customize it, and fit it to your character, or create the skeleton manually.

  2. [Optional] Add twist bones

    n-Panel > RigTools > Tools > Add Twist Bones Create twist bones on the arm, legs, chest, and neck as desired. These can also be created manually. See twist bones for more information.

  3. Weight paint the character

    Weight paint the character as you normally would. This can be done manually or with standard Blender tools. The weight paint proxy tool might help in some niche cases.

  4. Create the ORG bones

    n-Panel > RigTools > Tools > Generate ORG Bones See Generate ORG Bones for more details. This tool duplicates every DEF bone and creates a Copy Transforms constraint from the ORG bone to the DEF bone.

  5. Create the Torso assembly

    n-Panel > RigTools > Forward Kinematics > Torso Select the torso bones, neck, and head (excluding twist bones) and create the torso assembly. See torso assembly

  6. Create the Arm and Leg assemblies

    n-Panel > RigTools > Inverse Kinematics > Arm and Leg See ik_assemblies for more information

  7. Create additional assemblies as desired.

    Add shoulder, palm, and finger assemblies if desired. Add assemblies for hair, cloth, tails, etc. Use "FK only" for short detail chains, or "Simple FK" if you want tweak controls.

docs.title: Create Twist Bones
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Creates a chain of twist bones on each selected DEF bone.

Where: n-Panel > RigTools > Tools > Create Twist Bones (Edit or Pose mode)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Splits each selected DEF bone into a chain of twist bones, and assigns them as twist bones of the original bone. Use this before weight painting, so the twist bones can be weight painted along with the rest of the rig.

Twist bones are usually created on the upper arms, forearms, thighs, shins, chest, and neck. See Twist Bones for more information.

  • Only DEF bones (names starting with DEF-) are processed. Other selected bones are skipped.
  • Bones that already have the requested number of twist bones are skipped.
  • If a bone already has twist bones, but a different number, the tool stops with an error.

The twist bones are created as deform bones in the same bone collections as the original bone. The original bone isn't changed, including its deform setting.

Tip

After the twist bones are created, run Generate ORG Bones. The ORG twist bones are created and assigned automatically.

image/create_twist_bones.png — An upper arm and forearm in Edit mode after Create Twist Bones, showing the twist bones running along each bone.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Twist Bone Count: the number of twist bones created on each bone. Default: 2. Minimum: 2.

Note

The Arm and Leg assemblies use 4 twist bones by default. Use the same count here, or change the count in the assembly to match.

docs.title: Generate ORG Bones
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Creates an ORG bone for every DEF bone, and links the DEF bones to follow the ORG bones.

Where: n-Panel > RigTools > Tools > Generate ORG Bones

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Assemblies are built on ORG bones, not on the deform bones directly. Generate ORG Bones duplicates each DEF bone as an ORG bone, with the same hierarchy, and adds a Copy Transforms constraint so the DEF bone follows its ORG bone. See ORG & DEF for why the rig is split this way.

It's safe to run Generate ORG Bones more than once. ORG bones that already exist aren't changed (other than making sure the DEF bone is linked to them), and only the missing ORG bones are created. This makes it easy to add new DEF bones to the rig later, such as an accessory or a skirt, and generate ORG bones for just those.

Twist bone and heel pivot assignments are copied from the DEF bones to the new ORG bones. See Twist Bones and Foot Roll.

Image placeholder

image/generate_org_bones.png — The Generate ORG Bones dialog with its default settings.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Bone Selection: which DEF bones to process. Default: Selected Bones.
    • Selected Bones: only the selected DEF bones. Requires Edit or Pose mode.
    • Visible Bones: all visible DEF bones.
    • All Bones: all DEF bones in the armature.
  • DEF Bone Name: the naming template used to find DEF bones. Default: DEF-{name} (from the addon preferences).
  • Target Bone Name: the naming template for the new ORG bones. Default: ORG-{name} (from the addon preferences).
  • Relationship Type: how the DEF bones follow the ORG bones. Default: Copy Transforms.
    • Copy Transforms: the DEF bone gets a Copy Transforms constraint targeting its ORG bone. The DEF hierarchy is left alone.
    • Parent/Child: the DEF bone is parented to its ORG bone.
  • DEF Bone Collection: the name used for DEF bone collections. Default: DEF.
  • Target Bone Collection: the name used for ORG bone collections. Default: ORG.
  • Copy Collection Structure: copy the DEF bone collections for the ORG bones, replacing "DEF" with "ORG" in the collection names. For example, bones in DEF.Skirt go into ORG.Skirt. When disabled, all ORG bones go into a single collection. Default: on.
  • Disable To Bone Deform: turn off deform on the new ORG bones, so only the DEF bones deform the mesh. Default: on.

.L / .R suffixes are always kept at the end of the name, so DEF-forearm.L becomes ORG-forearm.L.

docs.title: RigTools Human Skeleton
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Adds a new human DEF skeleton, ready to fit to a character.

Where: Add > Armature > RigTools Human Skeleton (Object mode)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Creates a new armature at the 3D cursor with a basic humanoid deform skeleton. The bones are named and parented the way the RigTools templates expect, so the skeleton can go straight into the workflow after it's fit to the character.

The skeleton includes:

  • A root bone and a property bone.
  • Hips, two spine bones, chest, neck, and head.
  • Shoulders, arms, forearms, and hands.
  • Palms, three-bone fingers, and three-bone thumbs (optional).
  • Thighs, shins, feet, and toes.
  • Heel pivots for both feet, already assigned for foot roll.

The deform bones are placed in a DEF bone collection, the root and property bones in Root, and the heel pivots in PIVOT.

The skeleton doesn't include twist bones. Add them with Create Twist Bones after fitting the skeleton, if desired.

docs.text:
• Height: the total height of the skeleton. Default: about 1.65 m.
  • Pose: the arm pose. Default: A-Pose.
    • A-Pose: arms lowered 45 degrees.
    • T-Pose: arms horizontal.
  • Include Fingers: create the palm, finger, and thumb bones. Default: on.
  • Apply Root Widgets: add widgets to the root and property bones. See Apply Root Widgets. Default: on.

Tip

Use X-Axis Mirror in Edit mode while fitting the skeleton to keep the left and right sides matched.

docs.title: Parent Along Chain
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Parents the selected bones into chains, based on where their heads and tails meet.

Where: n-Panel > RigTools > Tools > Parent Along Chain (Edit mode)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Assemblies only care about parenting, so bones that line up end to end but aren't parented won't be recognized as a chain. This tool fixes that. For each selected bone, it looks for another selected bone whose tail sits on its head, and parents the bone to it.

Many chains can be fixed at once. Select all of the bones in all of the chains, and run the tool.

A bone is skipped (and reported) when:

  • More than one selected bone's tail is close enough to its head. The tool can't tell which one should be the parent.
  • Parenting it would create a loop.

Bones with nothing close enough are left alone. These are usually the first bone of each chain.

Image placeholder

image/parent_along_chain.png — Before/after Edit mode view of several unparented skirt bones (no relationship lines) and the same bones parented into chains (relationship lines visible).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Scan Distance: how close a bone's tail must be to another bone's head to be parented. Increase this if the bones don't line up exactly. Default: 0.0001 m.
  • Parent Connected: connect each bone to its new parent, locking its head to the parent's tail. Default: off.

docs.title: Rename Chain(s)
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Renames one or more selected chains using a template, with a number or letter for each chain and each bone.

Where: n-Panel > RigTools > Tools > Rename Chain(s) (Edit or Pose mode)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Renaming dozens of skirt or hair bones by hand is tedious. This tool renames every bone in the selected chains in one step. For example, with the default template bone.{chain}.{bone}, three skirt chains become:

  • bone.a.01, bone.a.02, bone.a.03, ...
  • bone.b.01, bone.b.02, bone.b.03, ...
  • bone.c.01, bone.c.02, bone.c.03, ...

With only one chain selected, {chain} isn't replaced, so leave it out of the template (for example, ponytail.{bone}).

Bones are numbered from the root of each chain toward the tip. When multiple chains are selected, the chains are ordered the same way as the Weight Paint Proxy, and the order is shown in the viewport while the dialog is open.

Tip

Include the DEF- prefix and side suffix in the template when renaming deform bones, for example DEF-skirt.{chain}.{bone}, so Generate ORG Bones can find them.

Image placeholder

image/rename_chain.png — The Rename Chain(s) dialog with several skirt chains selected, and the chain order letters drawn in the viewport next to each chain.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Name Template: the template for the new names. {chain} is replaced with the chain's number or letter, and {bone} with the bone's number or letter. Default: bone.{chain}.{bone}.
  • Chain Name Type: how chains are numbered. Only shown when more than one chain is selected. Default: Lowercase Letter.
  • Bone Name Type: how bones are numbered. Default: 2 Digit.

The name types are:

  • 2 Digit: 01, 02, 03, ...
  • 3 Digit: 001, 002, 003, ...
  • Lowercase Letter: a, b, c, ...
  • Uppercase Letter: A, B, C, ...

The chain order settings (Order Mode, Order Axis, Order Start Angle, Order Invert) are the same as the Weight Paint Proxy.

docs.title: Weight Paint Proxy
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Creates a simple mesh from the selected bone chains, with starting weights, to help weight paint chains like skirts, capes, and hair.

Where: n-Panel > RigTools > Tools > Weight Paint Proxy (Edit or Pose mode)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Automatic weights often struggle with cloth and hair chains, especially when the chains are close together like a skirt. The weight paint proxy is a stand-in mesh built directly from the bones. It gets a vertex at each joint, a vertex group for each bone, and starting weights that blend between neighboring bones. The proxy can be cleaned up in Weight Paint mode, then the weights transferred to the real mesh (for example, with a Data Transfer modifier).

With multiple chains selected, the chains can be stitched together into a single surface, like a skirt or a cape. The chains can also be stitched into a closed loop, like a skirt that goes all the way around.

When the tool runs, it switches to Weight Paint mode on the new proxy so you can start painting right away.

This tool might help in some niche cases. For most characters, standard weight painting is all that's needed.

Note

The proxy is flagged as a helper object, so it's ignored by the Visibility panel.

Image placeholder

image/weight_paint_proxy.png — A skirt's bone chains with a stitched, closed-loop weight paint proxy in Weight Paint mode, showing the blended weights for one bone.

docs.title: Chain order
docs.text:
To stitch chains together, the tool needs to know which chain is next to which. While the dialog is open, the order of the chains is shown in the viewport as numbers next to the first bone of each chain.

  • Order Mode: Angular orders the chains by their angle around the center of the selection (good for skirts). Linear orders the chains along an axis (good for capes or bangs).
  • Order Axis: the axis to rotate around (Angular) or sort along (Linear). Default: Z.
  • Order Start Angle: the angle where the first chain starts (Angular only). Default: 0.
  • Order Invert: reverse the order.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Stitch Chain: join multiple chains into a single surface. When disabled, each chain is a separate line of vertices. Default: on.
  • Chain Align: when chains have different lengths, which end lines up. Start lines up the roots; End lines up the tips. Only shown when the chains are different lengths. Default: Start.
  • Close Loop: stitch the last chain back to the first. Default: on.
  • Object Name: the name of the new object. {armature} is replaced with the name of the armature. Default: WProxy-{armature}.
  • Seed Weights: create vertex groups for each bone, with each joint weighted fully to its bone. Default: on.
  • Spread Weights: blend the weights between neighboring vertices. Default: on.
    • Spread Along Chain: how much weight spreads up and down each chain. Default: 0.10.
    • Spread Across Chain: how much weight spreads to neighboring chains. Default: 0.10.
    • Iterations: how many times to repeat the spread. More iterations give smoother, wider blending. Default: 1.
    • Lock Root Rows: the number of rows at the root of the chains that don't spread weight along the chain. Keeps the top of a skirt firmly attached. Default: 1.
  • Armature Modifier: add an Armature modifier to the proxy. Default: on.

docs.title: Rig UI (Collections)
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Buttons for showing and hiding the rig's bone collections.

Where: n-Panel > Item > Rig UI (armature, or a mesh deformed by the armature)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Rig UI panel shows a toggle button for each bone collection, so animators can quickly hide or show FK controls, IK controls, tweaks, and so on. It works with the armature selected, and also with one of the character's meshes selected.

New bone collections are added to the bottom of the panel automatically. Bone collections whose parent collection is hidden in Blender aren't shown.

The button layout is stored on the armature, so it's saved with the rig and shared with anyone who uses it. The layout is separate from Blender's bone collection list; rearranging or hiding buttons in the Rig UI doesn't change the order or visibility of the bone collections themselves.

Image placeholder

image/rig_ui_collections.png — The Rig UI panel for a finished character, with the collection buttons arranged into rows (e.g. Torso; Arm.FK.L / Arm.FK.R; Arm.IK.L / Arm.IK.R; tweaks) and gaps between groups.

docs.title: Assembly bone collections
docs.text:
Assemblies put their controls into bone collections named after the limb and side. For example, an arm on the left side creates collections for its FK controls, IK controls, and tweaks, such as Arm.FK.L, Arm.IK.L, and Arm.Tweak.L. Mechanism bones go into MCH collections, grouped under a parent MCH collection.

Assemblies that share a limb name and side share the same collections. For example, the left shoulder goes in with the left arm, and the left palm and fingers share the left hand collections.

The collections for a limb can be renamed from the Assembly Panel. Click the collection icon next to the assembly name, and enter the new names. The Rig UI layout is updated to match.

docs.title: Editing the layout
docs.text:
Click Edit to rearrange the buttons. In edit mode, clicking a button selects it instead of toggling the collection. With a button selected:

Button Action Gap Add a gap (blank space) above the selected row. Row up / Row down Move the collection to its own row above or below. Join up / Join down Move the collection onto the row above or below. ◀ / ▶ Move the collection left or right within its row. ▾ menu Rename the bone collection, or Hide/Show it in the Rig UI.

Gaps can be selected, moved with Row up / Row down, and removed with the X button next to them.

Renaming from the Rig UI renames the actual bone collection, and keeps the assemblies that use it up to date. Everything else in edit mode only changes the layout.

Hidden collections are shown greyed out in edit mode, and aren't shown at all outside of edit mode. Hiding is useful for collections that animators should never need, like MCH, ORG, and DEF.

Click Edit again to finish editing.

Image placeholder

image/rig_ui_edit.png — The Rig UI panel in edit mode, with one collection selected and the row/join/shift buttons, its dropdown menu, and a selected gap visible.

docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Shows the animator controls for the selected limb: FK/IK switching, IK parents, rotation follow, and so on.

Where: n-Panel > Item > Rig Properties (armature selected)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Rig Properties panel shows the properties for every assembly that the selected bones belong to. Select a hand control, and the arm's properties are shown. Select several controls, and the properties for each limb are shown together, grouped by limb (for example, "Left Arm" and "Right Arm"). When X-Axis Mirror is enabled in Pose mode, the opposite limb is shown as well.

The properties are stored on the property bone, so they can be keyframed like any other custom property. When auto keying is on, clicking one of the buttons next to a property inserts a keyframe.

Image placeholder

image/rig_properties.png — The Rig Properties panel with an arm control selected, showing FK > IK Switch, IK Stretch, FK Rotation Follow, and IK Parent, plus the IK > FK / FK > IK snap buttons.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Most properties are a slider with buttons next to it. The buttons set the property all the way to one side; the slider allows anything in between.

Property Buttons Description FK > IK Switch FK / IK Switches the limb between FK and IK. See FK/IK Switching. IK Stretch Off / On Allows the IK chain to stretch past its full length. See Standard IK. FK Rotation Follow Off / On Whether the first FK control follows its parent's rotation. See Rotation Isolation. The torso has separate Neck and Head versions. Leg Collision Off / On Turns skirt collision on or off. See Skirt Collision. Leg Ride Off / On Turns skirt ride on or off. See Skirt Ride. IK Parent (dropdown) What the IK controls follow. See IK Parent Switching.

docs.title: Snapping
docs.text:
Arm and Leg assemblies include FK <> IK snapping. Two buttons are shown below the limb's properties:

  • IK > FK: moves the IK control and pole to match the current FK pose, then switches the limb to IK.
  • FK > IK: rotates the FK controls to match the current IK pose, then switches the limb to FK.

Use these when changing modes mid-animation, so the limb doesn't jump.

Note

Snapping is not available for the spline IK assemblies. A spline IK pose often can't be matched by an FK chain.

Tip

Snapping doesn't insert keyframes. Keyframe the controls and the FK > IK Switch property after snapping.

Info

Shows and hides the character's meshes, mask modifiers, and solidify modifiers.

Where: n-Panel > Item > Visibility

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
With the armature selected, the Visibility panel lists every mesh that belongs to the rig: meshes parented to the armature, and meshes deformed by it. Each mesh has an eye button to show or hide it. This is handy for hiding clothing or hair that's in the way while animating.

Meshes with Mask modifiers get their own box, with a toggle for each mask modifier. Mask modifiers are often used to hide parts of the body that are under clothing. A mask modifier named like Mask-Shirt is shown as "Shirt".

If any of the meshes have Solidify modifiers, a Toggle Solidify button turns them all on or off at once. Solidify is often turned off while animating to keep the viewport fast.

With a mesh selected instead of the armature, the panel shows that mesh's mask modifiers and solidify toggle.

Tip

Modifiers whose names start with an underscore (_) are ignored by the Visibility panel. Use this for modifiers that animators shouldn't touch.

docs.title: Finger Curl
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Adds a single curl control to a finger, similar to Rigify's finger controls. Used by the Finger (Curl) assembly.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Creates a large control over the finger. The control works like an FK control for the whole finger: rotating it rotates the finger from the base. Scaling the control along its length curls the finger:

  • Scale down: the finger curls into a fist.
  • Scale back to 1.0: the finger straightens.

The individual FK controls and tweaks can still be posed on top of the curl.

The Finger (Curl) assembly also creates an FK Tweak Chain without a tweak at the base of the finger.

Image placeholder

image/finger_curl.png — A hand with Finger (Curl) assemblies, showing the paddle-shaped curl controls over each finger, with one curl control scaled down so its finger is curled.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Finger Curl Axis: the axis the finger curls around. Default: Auto.
    • Auto: detects the direction from the bend in the finger. If the finger is completely straight, it uses X.
    • X, -X, Z, -Z: curl around this axis of the finger bones. Use these if Auto curls the finger the wrong way.
  • FK Widget: the custom bone shape to use for FK controls. Default: CIRCLE. See widgets.
  • Add Tweak Bones / Skip First Tweak: see FK Tweak Chain.

Tip

Model the fingers with a slight natural curl. This helps Auto pick the correct curl direction.

docs.title: FK/IK Switching
docs.text: Builds the FK/IK blend mechanism so a limb can switch between FK and IK control stacks.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Creates the primary mechanism for switching between FK and IK setups. Creates a custom property on the property bone. The RigUI Properties will display this property as a float slider with FK/IK radio buttons next to it. This makes it easy to switch between FK and IK, while still giving full animator control for transitioning between them.

This tool creates the final FK chain and controls, but doesn't create the IK chain. It creates MCH-IK bones that will be controlled by an IK chain created in a later step. See standard IK and spline IK for IK chain creation.

  • FK End Widget: the custom bone shape for the last FK control in the chain (the hand or foot). Default: CIRCLE. See widgets.

docs.title: FK Tweak Chain
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Creates an FK chain with tweak controls at each joint.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Creates an FK control for each bone in the chain, plus a small tweak control at each joint. An additional tweak is added at the end of the chain. Moving a tweak stretches the bones on either side of it, which lets the animator adjust the deformation after the FK (or IK) pose is set.

This is used by the Simple FK, Skirt FK, Tail, and Finger assemblies. The IK assemblies, the torso, and the twist bones use the same tweak controls.

See FK Chain for an FK chain without tweak controls.

Image placeholder

image/fk_tweak_chain.png — A 3-4 bone chain in Pose mode showing the FK widgets and the small sphere tweak widgets at each joint, including the extra tweak at the end of the chain. Ideally one tweak is moved so the stretch is visible.

docs.title: Skip first tweak
docs.text: When Skip First Tweak is enabled, no tweak is created at the start of the chain. The Finger assemblies use this so the base of the finger doesn't get a tweak control sitting on top of the knuckle.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Add Tweak Bones: create the tweak controls. When disabled, the assembly creates an FK only chain. Default: on.
  • FK Widget: the custom bone shape to use for FK controls. Default: CIRCLE. See widgets.
  • Skip First Tweak: don't create a tweak at the start of the chain. Default: off (on for the Finger assemblies).

docs.title: Foot Roll
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Adds a foot roll control to the IK foot, for rolling onto the heel or the ball of the foot, and rocking side to side. Used by the Leg assembly.

Requires

A heel pivot bone assigned to the foot · at least one bone past the foot (the toe)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Creates a roll control attached to the IK foot control. Rotating the roll control:

  • Forward/back (X rotation): rolls the foot onto the heel in one direction, and onto the ball of the foot in the other. When rolling onto the ball, the toe stays planted on the ground.
  • Side to side (Z rotation): rocks the foot onto its inside or outside edge.

The roll control's location and scale are locked. The IK foot control is moved down to the ground, from the heel to the tip of the toe, so it's easier to see and select.

Image placeholder

image/foot_roll.png — A leg in IK mode showing the flattened IK foot control on the ground and the roll control behind the heel. Ideally a second shot with the roll control rotated so the foot is up on the ball with the toe planted.

docs.title: Heel pivot
docs.text:
The heel pivot is a bone that tells the foot roll where the heel is. It should sit at the back of the heel, on the ground, and run across the width of the foot. The ends of the heel pivot are used as the pivot points when the foot rocks side to side.

The heel pivot is assigned to the foot bone (not the toe) in Bone Properties > Rig Tools > Heel Pivot. The RigTools Human Skeleton includes heel pivots that are already assigned.

Heel pivots can be assigned to the DEF foot bones before creating the ORG bones. Generate ORG Bones copies the assignment to the ORG foot.

Image placeholder

image/heel_pivot.png — Edit mode view of a foot showing where the heel pivot bone should be placed (at the back of the heel, on the ground, spanning the width of the foot), plus the Heel Pivot field in Bone Properties > Rig Tools.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: • Add Foot Roll: add the foot roll control. Default: on for the Leg assembly.

docs.title: IK Parent Switching
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Lets the animator choose what the IK controls follow: the root, the torso, the hips, the chest, the head, and so on.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Creates a custom property on the property bone. The Rig Properties panel displays it as IK Parent, a dropdown with one entry per parent. The IK control and the pole both follow the selected parent. For spline IK, all of the spline controls follow the selected parent.

For example, with an arm set to Chest, the hand stays in place relative to the chest as the torso moves. Set to Root, the hand stays planted in the world while the body moves around it.

Warning

Changing the IK parent does not compensate for the change. The IK controls will jump to their new position relative to the new parent.

The default parents for each template come from the bone names in the Armature Settings. The torso creates the torso, hips, chest, and head bones, so it needs to be set up before the IK assemblies.

Assembly Default parents Arm Root, Torso, Hips, Chest, Head Leg Root, Torso, Foot Skirt - Spline Root, Torso, Hips Hair - Spline Root, Torso, Head Tail - Spline Root, Torso, Hips

docs.title: IK control as pole parent
docs.text: The Leg assembly adds a Foot option. When Foot is selected, the knee pole follows the IK foot control, so the knee points wherever the foot points. The IK foot control itself follows the root. This is the default for legs.

docs.title: Changing IK parents
docs.text:
IK parents can be changed without reconfiguring the assembly. Select a bone in the assembly, then click IK Parents in the Assembly Panel. The dialog lets you:

  • Add, remove, or rename parents. Any bone in the armature can be used as a parent.
  • Enable or disable Add IK Control as Pole Parent, and set its label.

The animator's current selection is kept where possible.

Image placeholder

image/ik_parents_dialog.png — The IK Parents dialog opened from the Assembly Panel for a leg, showing the label/bone rows, Add Parent button, and the "Add IK Control as Pole Parent" option with the "Foot" label.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Setup IK Parent Switching: enable IK parent switching. Default: on for Skirt - Spline, Hair - Spline, and Tail - Spline. Always on for Arm and Leg.
  • IK Parents: the list of parents. Each parent has a label (shown in the Rig Properties dropdown) and a bone.

docs.title: Master Controllers
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Adds controls that rotate a group of FK bones at once. Useful for curling tails, hair, and cloth with a single control.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Master controllers come in two types:

  • Use FK Bones (FK follow): an existing FK control acts as the master. When it rotates, the FK controls after it rotate by the same amount, which curls the rest of the chain. No extra controls are created. See Rotation Follow.
  • Add Dedicated Masters: a separate, larger master control is created for each group. Rotating, moving, or scaling the master moves every FK control in its group, including the first one. The individual FK controls can still be posed on top of that.

Each FK control still works normally. The master controllers add on top of the animator's FK pose.

The chain can be split into groups with an interval, so a long tail can have a master every few bones instead of one for the whole chain.

Image placeholder

image/master_controllers.png — A Tail assembly in Pose mode with dedicated master controls (every 3 bones). One master is rotated, showing its group of FK controls curling together.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Create FK Master Controllers / FK Follow: enable master controllers. Default: on for Simple FK, FK Only, Skirt FK, Tail, Finger (FK), and the spline assemblies. Off for Arm, Leg, Finger (Curl), and Shoulder.
  • Type: the type of master controller. Default: Use FK Bones (Add Dedicated Masters for Skirt FK, Tail, and Tail - Spline).
    • Use FK Bones: existing FK controls act as masters (FK follow).
    • Add Dedicated Masters: separate master controls are created.
  • Spacing: how the chain is divided.
    • Single Controller: one master for the whole chain.
    • Interval: a new master every Interval bones. Default interval: 3 (minimum 2).
  • Skip First: leave the first bone of the chain out of the master controllers. The second bone becomes the first master. Default: on for all templates.
  • Master Controller Widget: the custom bone shape for dedicated masters. Only shown when the type is Add Dedicated Masters. Default: CIRCLE (RECTANGLE for skirts). See widgets.

Tip

Skip First is useful when the first bone acts as an anchor, like the base of a tail or the top of a skirt. For fingers, it lets the second knuckle curl the finger without moving the knuckle at the base.

docs.title: Palm
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Creates FK controls for the palm bones, with the index and pinky palms acting as controls for the palm bones between them. Used by the Palm assembly.

Requires

Palm bones selected (one per finger) · usually children of the hand

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The palm bones (sometimes called metacarpals) are not a chain. They are usually siblings, all parented to the hand. So unlike the other assemblies, the palm is created from a selection of individual bones, one per finger. Both hands can be selected at the same time.

Each palm bone gets an FK control. The first palm (usually the index) and the last palm (usually the pinky) act as controls for the palm bones between them: rotating the index or pinky palm also rotates the middle palms, fading out toward the other side of the hand. This makes cupping and spreading the hand easy with only two controls. The middle palm controls can still be posed on top of that.

Image placeholder

image/palm.png — A hand with a Palm assembly, showing the pill-shaped FK controls on each palm bone, with the pinky palm rotated so the hand cups and the middle palms follow partway.

docs.title: Palm order
docs.text:
Since the palm bones aren't a chain, the Palm assembly opens a dialog to confirm the order of the bones, from index to pinky. The order can be set by:

  • Name: the trailing letter or number in the bone names (for example, palm.A, palm.B, ...). Only available when all of the selected bones have one.
  • X, Y, Z: the position of the bones along that axis.
  • Manual: use the arrow buttons to move bones up or down the list.

Reverse flips the order. When both hands are selected, the left and right bones are shown side by side and must mirror each other.

Image placeholder

image/palm_order.png — The Palm dialog showing the Order section with Name/X/Y/Z/Manual, Reverse, and the Left/Right columns with up/down arrows.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Index Falloff Type: how quickly the first palm's (index) rotation fades across the middle palms. Default: Sharp.
  • Pinky Falloff Type: how quickly the last palm's (pinky) rotation fades across the middle palms. Default: Linear.
  • FK Widget: the custom bone shape to use for the palm FK controls. Default: PILL. See widgets.

See Twist Bones (tool) for a description of the falloff types. The palm also offers a None falloff, which turns off that side's influence on the middle palms.

docs.title: Rotation Follow
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Makes the FK controls further down a chain follow the rotation of an earlier FK control. This is the "Use FK Bones" type of master controller, often called "FK follow".

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
With FK follow, rotating an FK control also rotates the FK controls after it by the same amount. Rotating the base of a tail by 10 degrees bends every following bone by 10 degrees as well, so the whole tail curls instead of swinging as a straight line.

The following FK controls can still be rotated on their own. Their rotation is added on top of what they pick up from the master.

FK follow is the default for Simple FK, FK Only, Finger (FK), Hair - Spline, and Skirt - Spline. With Skip First enabled (the default), the second FK control is the master, so the first bone can be posed without curling the rest of the chain.

With an interval, each master only drives the bones up to the next master. See Master Controllers for the full set of parameters.

Note

This is not the same as the FK Rotation Follow property in the Rig Properties panel. That property is part of rotation isolation, and controls whether the first FK control follows its parent.

Image placeholder

image/rotation_follow.png — A Simple FK hair strand with the second FK control rotated, showing the rest of the strand curling with it.

docs.title: Rotation Isolation
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Lets the first FK control of a chain choose whether or not to follow its parent's rotation.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Normally, when a parent bone rotates, its children rotate with it. Rotation isolation adds a switch so the first FK control of the chain can ignore its parent's rotation, while still moving with it. For example, with an isolated arm, rotating the chest will carry the shoulder joint with it, but the arm will keep pointing in the same direction.

This creates a custom property on the property bone. The Rig Properties panel displays it as FK Rotation Follow, a slider with On/Off buttons next to it:

  • On (1.0): the FK control follows its parent's rotation. This is the default.
  • Off (0.0): the FK control's rotation is isolated from its parent.

Values in between blend the two.

The torso has separate rotation isolation for the neck and the head. These show up as Neck FK Rotation Follow and Head FK Rotation Follow.

Note

Rotation isolation only affects the FK controls. IK controls already ignore the rotation of the chain's parent. See IK parent switching for choosing what the IK controls follow.

Image placeholder

image/rotation_isolation.png — Side-by-side of an FK arm with the chest rotated: on the left with FK Rotation Follow on (arm swings with the chest), on the right with it off (arm keeps its world orientation).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Add Rotation Isolation: add the rotation isolation switch to the first FK control. Default: on for Arm, Leg, Skirt FK, Tail, and the spline assemblies. Off for Simple FK and FK Only.
  • Inherit Scale From Root: the FK chain takes its scale from the root bone instead of the chain's parent. Scaling the chest, for example, won't scale the arm. Only shown when rotation isolation is enabled. Default: on for Arm, off for Leg.

The torso has the same options for the neck and the head:

  • Add Neck Rotation Isolation / Add Head Rotation Isolation. Default: on.
  • Neck Inherit Scale From Root / Head Inherit Scale From Root. Default: on.

Creates a single FK control for a humanoid shoulder (clavicle). Used by the Shoulder assembly.

The shoulder bone selected · usually parented to the chest

The shoulder is grouped with the arm on the same side. Its control shows up in both the arm's FK and IK bone collections, so it's available no matter which mode the arm is in.

Create the shoulder before or after the Arm assembly. Select only the shoulder bone; the arm should be a separate assembly.

docs.title: Skirt Collision
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Pushes skirt chains out of the way of the legs, so the legs don't poke through the skirt.

Requires

Leg assemblies set up first (recommended) · or thigh bones picked manually

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Each bone in the skirt chain is kept outside of the nearest thigh. When the leg swings forward into the skirt, the skirt chain is pushed forward with it. The FK controls can still be posed on top of the collision.

Skirt collision works on the FK side of the chain. On the Skirt - Spline assembly, collision only applies while the skirt is in FK.

The collision can be turned on and off by the animator with the Leg Collision property in the Rig Properties panel. Collision is on by default.

Image placeholder

image/skirt_collision.png — A Skirt FK assembly with one leg raised forward, showing the skirt chains in front of the thigh pushed outward instead of passing through the leg.

docs.title: Skirt legs
docs.text:
Skirt collision needs to know which bones are the legs. When a skirt assembly is created, the Skirt Legs list is filled in automatically with the thigh of every Leg assembly in the rig. Thighs can be added or removed from the list in the redo panel.

Tip

Set up both legs with the Leg assembly before creating the skirt, and the skirt legs will be filled in for you.

docs.title: Collision influence
docs.text:
After the assembly is created, the collision strength of each bone in the skirt chain can be adjusted in the Assembly Panel. Each bone has a slider from 0 to 1 (values up to 2 can be typed in). A value of 0 turns collision off for that bone; values above 1 push the skirt further out.

These values are kept when the assembly is reconfigured.

Image placeholder

image/skirt_collision_influence.png — The Assembly Panel for a skirt assembly, showing the Skirt Collision sliders for each bone in the chain.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Add Skirt Collision: add skirt collision to the chain. Default: on for Skirt FK and Skirt - Spline.
  • Skirt Legs: the thigh bones the skirt collides with. Filled in automatically from the Leg assemblies.

docs.title: Skirt Ride
docs.text:
Info

This is AI-generated documentation that has not yet been human reviewed.

Makes short skirts ride up when a leg is lifted.

Requires

Leg assemblies set up first (recommended) · or thigh bones picked manually

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
When a leg is lifted, a short skirt tends to get pulled up with it. Skirt ride shortens the top bone of each skirt chain as the thigh swings forward, which raises the rest of the chain. Chains closest to the front of the lifted leg ride up the most; chains on the far side of the skirt aren't affected.

Skirt ride is intended for short skirts. It's disabled by default, and is usually not needed for longer skirts and dresses. It can be combined with skirt collision.

Skirt ride works on the FK side of the chain. On the Skirt - Spline assembly, ride only applies while the skirt is in FK.

The ride can be turned on and off by the animator with the Leg Ride property in the Rig Properties panel. Ride is on by default when it's been added.

Image placeholder

image/skirt_ride.png — A short Skirt FK assembly with one thigh lifted forward, comparing Leg Ride on (front chains shortened and raised) vs. off.

docs.title: Skirt legs
docs.text: Skirt ride uses the same Skirt Legs list as skirt collision. When skirt ride is enabled, each leg also has a Forward Axis: the axis of the thigh bone that points forward, toward the front of the character. This is detected automatically, and usually doesn't need to be changed. If the skirt rides up when the leg moves backward instead of forward, try the opposite axis.

docs.title: Ride influence
docs.text:
Each skirt chain gets a ride influence for each leg, based on where the chain sits around the thigh. After the assembly is created, these can be adjusted in the Assembly Panel. Each leg has a slider from 0 to 2 (higher values can be typed in). Higher values make the chain ride up more for the same leg lift.

These values are kept when the assembly is reconfigured.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• Add Skirt Ride: add skirt ride to the chain. Default: off.
  • Skirt Legs: the thigh bones that make the skirt ride up, with the forward axis of each thigh. Filled in automatically from the Leg assemblies.
